content: Serology is the scientific discipline that focuses on the study of blood serum, which is the clear, yellowish fluid that remains after blood has clotted and the blood cells have been removed. In clinical practice, the term serology is most commonly associated with the diagnostic detection and identification of antibodies present in the serum. Antibodies detected through serological testing are typically produced by the immune system in response to specific stimuli. These stimuli may include infections caused by microorganisms, the introduction of foreign proteins into the body (such as during a mismatched blood transfusion), or the presence of the body’s own proteins in cases of autoimmune diseases. Serological tests are frequently employed for diagnostic purposes when an infection is suspected. They are also used in the evaluation of rheumatic diseases and in various other clinical scenarios, such as determining an individual’s blood type. These tests are particularly valuable in diagnosing patients with certain immune deficiencies, such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia, a condition characterized by the absence of antibody production. In such cases, serological tests for antibodies will consistently yield negative results due to the lack of antibody production. There are several serological techniques available, and the choice of method depends on the specific antibodies being studied. Common techniques include agglutination, precipitation, complement fixation, and the use of fluorescent-labeled antibodies. While serological tests are most commonly performed on blood serum, they are not exclusively limited to this fluid. Similar tests can also be conducted on other bodily fluids, such as semen and saliva, which share properties with serum. For example, serological analysis of semen can be used in forensic investigations to link a suspect to a semen sample, such as in cases of sexual assault.
